title: Quantum Computing with ket
text:
Preface
This book teaches quantum computing by doing it.
Every concept is introduced alongside runnable code using ket — a TypeScript quantum circuit simulator. You don’t need a physics degree. You need curiosity and a willingness to play with the examples.

title: Quantum Computing with ket
text:
How to read this book
The book is structured in three parts:
The Foundations (Chapters 1–4) covers the vocabulary of quantum computing: qubits, gates, superposition, and entanglement. These chapters assume no physics background — only familiarity with the idea of a computer program.
Algorithms (Chapters 5–8) shows why quantum computers are interesting: they can solve certain problems faster than any classical computer. We’ll build up to Shor’s algorithm, which can factor large numbers and is the reason quantum computers make cryptographers nervous.
Reality (Chapters 9–10) grounds everything in how quantum hardware actually behaves. Real qubits are noisy. We’ll see what that means and how to work with it.

title: Quantum Computing with ket
text:
The interactive examples
In the HTML version of this book, code blocks run live in your browser. Every visualization is produced by ket — no screenshots, no mock data. You can modify the code and re-run it.
In the PDF version, code is shown with its pre-rendered output.

title: Quantum Computing with ket
text:
A note on math
Quantum computing has precise mathematical foundations. This book uses that math when it clarifies rather than obscures. Key equations are introduced slowly, with plain-English translations. If you’ve seen a matrix before, you have enough math to read this book.

“If you think you understand quantum mechanics, you don’t understand quantum mechanics.” — Richard Feynman
(Feynman also said quantum computers might be the only way to simulate nature efficiently. That idea still drives the field.)

title: 1  From Bits to Qubits
text:
1.1 Superposition
A classical bit is a light switch — off (0) or on (1). Every computer you’ve ever used is built from billions of these, flipping furiously.
A qubit is stranger. Flip one and measure it: you get 0 or 1 with equal probability. Every time, random. But apply the same flip twice and you always get back exactly where you started. No classical random process can do that.
That’s interference. It’s what makes quantum computing interesting.
The Hadamard gate (h) takes a definite \(|0\rangle\) and puts it into equal superposition:
c_h = new ket.Circuit(1).h(0)
svg(c_h.simulate({ shots: 10000 }).toSVG())
50/50 — each run varies slightly due to sampling, but the true probability is exactly \(\frac{1}{2}\). Now apply it twice:
c_hh = new ket.Circuit(1).h(0).h(0)
svg(c_hh.simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())
Always |0⟩. The randomness cancels perfectly. This is interference — the defining feature that separates a qubit from a coin flip.

title: 1  From Bits to Qubits
text:
1.2 The math (briefly)
A qubit’s state is written as:
\[|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\]
\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are complex numbers called amplitudes. The probability of measuring 0 is \(|\alpha|^2\), and of measuring 1 is \(|\beta|^2\). They always sum to 1.
After h(0), both amplitudes are \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so both probabilities are \(\frac{1}{2}\).
You can read the amplitudes directly with stateAsArray():

new ket.Circuit(1).h(0).stateAsArray()






Both amplitudes are exactly \(1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707\), with phase 0. The prob column is \(|0.707|^2 = 0.5\). After a Z gate the probabilities don’t change — but the phase does:

new ket.Circuit(1).h(0).z(0).stateAsArray()






Same probabilities, but the \(|1\rangle\) amplitude is now \(-0.707\) (phase = \(\pi\)). Measurement can’t see this — but the next gate can. Phase is invisible to the observer, but real to the computation.
The notation \(|\cdot\rangle\) (a ket) is standard physics shorthand for a quantum state. This library is named after it.

title: 1  From Bits to Qubits
text:
1.3 Measurement collapses the state
Before you measure, the qubit is genuinely in superposition — not secretly one or the other. The moment you measure, it collapses to a definite 0 or 1 and the amplitude information is gone.
This is why H·H works: both gates interact with the amplitudes before any measurement. Once you measure, the phase is lost.
To see it: a measurement between the two H gates collapses the qubit to either \(|0\rangle\) or \(|1\rangle\). Then the second H acts on a classical state — and both H|0⟩ and H|1⟩ give 50/50, not the original certainty:

svg(new ket.Circuit(1).h(0).simulate({ shots: 10000 }).toSVG())







svg(new ket.Circuit(1).x(0).h(0).simulate({ shots: 10000 }).toSVG())






Both are 50/50 — the bars may differ by a percent or two from shot noise, but the underlying probability is exactly \(\frac{1}{2}\) in both cases. The second H has no memory of the first. Contrast with H·H, which always returns |0⟩.

title: 1  From Bits to Qubits
text:
1.4 Bits vs. qubits




Classical bit
Qubit




State
Always 0 or 1
Superposition until measured


Measurement effect
None
Collapses the state


Interference
No
Yes



A qubit doesn’t store more information than a classical bit — a measurement still yields one bit. The advantage is what you can do with amplitudes before measurement: steer interference toward right answers and away from wrong ones.
That’s the rest of this book.

title: 1  From Bits to Qubits
text:
1.5 What’s next
Chapter 2 introduces the Bloch sphere — a geometric picture of every possible single-qubit state — and the full set of single-qubit gates.

title: 2  Single-Qubit Gates
text:
2.1 The Bloch sphere
A qubit’s state is a point on a sphere.
Every single-qubit gate is a rotation of that sphere. This isn’t an analogy — it’s the geometry. Understanding it makes every gate intuitive.
The state \(|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\) has two real degrees of freedom (after accounting for normalisation and global phase). Two angles — \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) — are enough to pin down any single-qubit state:
\[|\psi\rangle = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}|0\rangle + e^{i\phi}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}|1\rangle\]
\(\theta\) runs from 0 (north pole, \(|0\rangle\)) to \(\pi\) (south pole, \(|1\rangle\)). \(\phi\) is the angle around the equator. Together they define a point on a unit sphere — the Bloch sphere.
svg(new ket.Circuit(1).blochSphere(0))
svg(new ket.Circuit(1).x(0).blochSphere(0))
svg(new ket.Circuit(1).h(0).blochSphere(0))
From left to right: \(|0\rangle\) (north pole), \(|1\rangle\) (south pole), \(H|0\rangle = |{+}\rangle\) (equator). The equator is equal superposition. Every point in between is a valid qubit state.

title: 2  Single-Qubit Gates
text:
2.2 The Pauli gates — axis flips
The three Pauli gates are 180° rotations around the three axes.
X rotates 180° around the X axis — the quantum NOT gate, swapping \(|0\rangle \leftrightarrow |1\rangle\):

svg(new ket.Circuit(1).x(0).blochSphere(0))







svg(new ket.Circuit(1).x(0).simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())






Z rotates 180° around the Z axis. It leaves \(|0\rangle\) unchanged but flips the sign of \(|1\rangle\): \(Z|1\rangle = -|1\rangle\). This is a phase flip — invisible to single-qubit measurement, but it changes how the state interferes in a larger circuit.
Y is X followed by Z (up to a global phase). Less common in introductory circuits, but completes the Pauli set.

title: 2  Single-Qubit Gates
text:
2.3 H revisited — a diagonal rotation
H is a 180° rotation around the axis halfway between X and Z. That’s why it maps poles to equator and back:

\(H|0\rangle = |{+}\rangle\) → equator
\(H|{+}\rangle = |0\rangle\) → back to north pole
\(HH = I\) — two 180° rotations around the same axis cancel

The last point explains Chapter 1’s interference result. H is its own inverse.

title: 2  Single-Qubit Gates
text:
2.4 Phase gates — spinning around Z
S and T are partial rotations around the Z axis: 90° and 45° respectively. They don’t change measurement probabilities — the state stays on the equator — but they shift the phase \(\phi\), which changes how the qubit interferes with others.

svg(new ket.Circuit(1).h(0).blochSphere(0))







svg(new ket.Circuit(1).h(0).t(0).blochSphere(0))







svg(new ket.Circuit(1).h(0).s(0).blochSphere(0))






Left to right: H|0⟩, T·H|0⟩ (+45°), S·H|0⟩ (+90°). Same latitude — same measurement probabilities — different phase.

title: 2  Single-Qubit Gates
text:
2.5 Rotation gates — arbitrary angles
rx, ry, rz rotate by any angle around each axis. The argument order is (angle, qubit).

svg(new ket.Circuit(1).rx(Math.PI / 4, 0).blochSphere(0))







svg(new ket.Circuit(1).rx(Math.PI / 2, 0).blochSphere(0))







svg(new ket.Circuit(1).rx(Math.PI, 0).blochSphere(0))






rx(π) is exactly X. rx(π/2) is halfway — a common building block on real hardware, where every gate is ultimately expressed as a combination of rz and ry rotations.

title: 2  Single-Qubit Gates
text:
2.7 What’s next
Chapter 3 adds a second qubit and introduces entanglement — the phenomenon that makes quantum computing qualitatively more powerful than anything classical.

title: 3  Multiple Qubits
text:
3.1 Two-qubit states
One qubit has two basis states: \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\).
Two qubits have four: \(|00\rangle\), \(|01\rangle\), \(|10\rangle\), \(|11\rangle\).
\(n\) qubits have \(2^n\) basis states — and a quantum state is a superposition over all of them simultaneously. This exponential state space is where quantum computing gets its leverage.
A two-qubit state is written:
\[|\psi\rangle = \alpha_{00}|00\rangle + \alpha_{01}|01\rangle + \alpha_{10}|10\rangle + \alpha_{11}|11\rangle\]
Four amplitudes, each complex, summing to 1 in squared magnitude. Putting both qubits in equal superposition with H gives all four outcomes equally likely:
c_2h = new ket.Circuit(2).h(0).h(1)
svg(c_2h.toSVG())
pre(c_2h.draw())
svg(c_2h.simulate({ shots: 2000 }).toSVG())
Each of the four basis states gets amplitude \(\frac{1}{2}\), probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). The histogram shows them equally distributed. With 3 qubits it would be 8 outcomes. With 10, 1024.

title: 3  Multiple Qubits
section: 3.2 Individual qubits are still independent here
text:
3.2 Individual qubits are still independent here
When there’s no two-qubit gate connecting them, each qubit evolves on its own. We can see this on the Bloch sphere — each qubit lives at its own point, independently:

c_ind = new ket.Circuit(2).h(0).x(1)
svg(c_ind.toSVG())















Qubit 0 is at the equator (superposition). Qubit 1 is at the south pole (\(|1\rangle\)).

svg(c_ind.blochSphere(0))







svg(c_ind.blochSphere(1))






Two different poles. The state is a product state — it factors as \(|{+}\rangle \otimes |1\rangle\). The qubits are completely independent.

title: 3  Multiple Qubits
text:
3.3 The CNOT gate
Single-qubit gates act on one qubit at a time. To create correlations between qubits, you need a two-qubit gate.
The CNOT (controlled-NOT) is the workhorse:

If the control is \(|0\rangle\), do nothing to the target
If the control is \(|1\rangle\), flip the target


svg(new ket.Circuit(2).cx(0, 1).toSVG())







pre(new ket.Circuit(2).cx(0, 1).draw())






The filled dot is the control; the ⊕ is the target. On classical inputs it’s just XOR. We can verify each row of the truth table by preparing each input state and measuring:

cnot_00 = new ket.Circuit(2).cx(0, 1)
svg(cnot_00.simulate({ shots: 500 }).toSVG())
















cnot_10 = new ket.Circuit(2).x(0).cx(0, 1)
svg(cnot_10.simulate({ shots: 500 }).toSVG())
















cnot_01 = new ket.Circuit(2).x(1).cx(0, 1)
svg(cnot_01.simulate({ shots: 500 }).toSVG())
















cnot_11 = new ket.Circuit(2).x(0).x(1).cx(0, 1)
svg(cnot_11.simulate({ shots: 500 }).toSVG())















Each histogram has a single bar — the classical inputs map deterministically to classical outputs. On superpositions, the CNOT does something more interesting, which is the subject of Chapter 4.

title: 3  Multiple Qubits
text:
3.4 Building up circuits
Gates chain left to right. Each is a matrix acting on the joint state vector. Here is a three-qubit circuit that puts each qubit through a different single-qubit gate:

c_3 = new ket.Circuit(3).h(0).x(1).rx(Math.PI / 3, 2)
svg(c_3.toSVG())
















pre(c_3.draw())







svg(c_3.simulate({ shots: 2000 }).toSVG())






Qubit 0 is in superposition (H), qubit 1 is always \(|1\rangle\) (X), qubit 2 has a partial rotation. The joint measurement reflects all three: the second bit is always 1, the other two vary.

title: 3  Multiple Qubits
text:
3.5 Product states have zero entanglement
When there are no two-qubit gates, the state is a product state and has no entanglement across any bond. bondEntropies() gives the log₂ entanglement entropy across each consecutive pair of qubits:

c_product = new ket.Circuit(4).h(0).x(1).h(2).rx(Math.PI/4, 3)
svg(c_product.toSVG())
















c_product.bondEntropies()






All zeros. No gate has connected any qubit to any other. Each qubit is an island. Chapter 4 shows what happens when CNOT introduces correlations — and how the entropy changes.

title: 3  Multiple Qubits
text:
3.6 Circuit depth and width
Two dimensions describe the cost of a quantum circuit:

Width — number of qubits (space)
Depth — longest path from input to output (time; determines exposure to noise)

Gates on separate qubits can run in parallel, reducing depth:

c_parallel = new ket.Circuit(3).h(0).h(1).h(2)
svg(c_parallel.toSVG())
















c_serial = new ket.Circuit(1).h(0).h(0).h(0)
svg(c_serial.toSVG())















The three-qubit version has depth 1 — all three H gates execute simultaneously. The single-qubit version has depth 3. Both apply three H gates total, but the three-qubit circuit finishes three times faster on hardware.
Real hardware runs gates in parallel where qubits don’t interact. Minimising depth is one of the key tasks in quantum compilation.

title: 3  Multiple Qubits
text:
3.7 What’s next
CNOT acting on a superposition creates something classical circuits can’t: entanglement. Chapter 4 explores what that means, how to measure it, and why it’s the engine behind every quantum speedup.

title: 4  Entanglement
text:
4.1 What entanglement is
Apply H to qubit 0, then CNOT with qubit 0 as control and qubit 1 as target:
Only \(|00\rangle\) and \(|11\rangle\). Never \(|01\rangle\) or \(|10\rangle\).
The two qubits are entangled. Measure one and you instantly know the other — perfectly correlated, no matter how far apart they are.
Before measurement, neither qubit has a definite value. The joint state is:
\[|\Phi^+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|00\rangle + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|11\rangle\]
This is a Bell state — the simplest maximally entangled state. It cannot be written as a product of two independent qubit states. There is no \(|\psi_0\rangle \otimes |\psi_1\rangle\) that equals it.
That factorability is the test: if you can write the state as a product, the qubits are independent. If you can’t, they’re entangled.

title: 4  Entanglement
text:
4.2 Entanglement entropy
There’s a quantitative measure. bondEntropies() returns the log₂ von Neumann entropy across each consecutive bond. A product state scores 0. Maximal entanglement scores 1.

product = new ket.Circuit(2).h(0).x(1)
product.bondEntropies()
















// Bell state: maximum entanglement
bell.bondEntropies()






The product state scores exactly 0. The Bell state scores exactly 1 — one full bit of entanglement entropy across the bond between qubit 0 and qubit 1. This is the physics. The histogram alone can’t tell you this; the entropy can.

title: 4  Entanglement
text:
4.3 Looking at the Bloch sphere
In a product state, each qubit has a well-defined Bloch vector:

svg(product.blochSphere(0))







svg(product.blochSphere(1))






Qubit 0 sits on the equator (superposition). Qubit 1 sits at the south pole (\(|1\rangle\)). Each qubit has a pure state of its own.
Now look at the same qubits in the Bell state:

svg(bell.blochSphere(0))







svg(bell.blochSphere(1))






Both qubits sit at the origin of the Bloch sphere — not on the surface, but at the centre. A point on the surface is a pure state. The centre is a maximally mixed state. Each qubit, viewed alone, is completely undetermined. The information lives only in the correlation between them.
This is the geometric signature of entanglement: entangled qubits have no individual Bloch vectors. The description of the pair cannot be reduced to descriptions of two individuals.

title: 4  Entanglement
text:
4.4 The four Bell states
There are four maximally entangled two-qubit states, one for each combination of relative phase and parity:
\[|\Phi^+\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle) \qquad |\Phi^-\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle - |11\rangle)\] \[|\Psi^+\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|01\rangle + |10\rangle) \qquad |\Psi^-\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|01\rangle - |10\rangle)\]

phi_plus  = new ket.Circuit(2).h(0).cx(0,1)
phi_minus = new ket.Circuit(2).h(0).cx(0,1).z(0)
psi_plus  = new ket.Circuit(2).h(0).cx(0,1).x(1)
psi_minus = new ket.Circuit(2).h(0).cx(0,1).x(1).z(0)






























svg(phi_plus.toSVG())







svg(phi_plus.simulate({ shots: 2000 }).toSVG())







svg(phi_minus.toSVG())







svg(phi_minus.simulate({ shots: 2000 }).toSVG())







svg(psi_plus.toSVG())







svg(psi_plus.simulate({ shots: 2000 }).toSVG())







svg(psi_minus.toSVG())







svg(psi_minus.simulate({ shots: 2000 }).toSVG())






\(\Phi^+\) and \(\Phi^-\) show only \(|00\rangle\)/\(|11\rangle\). \(\Psi^+\) and \(\Psi^-\) show only \(|01\rangle\)/\(|10\rangle\). The \(\pm\) phase difference is invisible in the histograms — it matters when these states enter further gates. All four score entropy = 1:

[phi_plus, phi_minus, psi_plus, psi_minus].map(c => c.bondEntropies())

title: 4  Entanglement
text:
4.5 Why it’s strange
The correlations are stronger than anything classical physics allows.
Imagine two coins that always land the same way — both heads or both tails — no matter how far apart they are. Classically, you’d explain this by assuming they were preset: heads-heads or tails-tails, decided before they separated. Hidden information.
Quantum mechanics rules this out. The Bell inequalities are a mathematical test: correlations from hidden preset values can only be so strong. Entangled particles violate them. The correlations are not pre-agreed — they’re genuinely created at the moment of measurement.
This is what Einstein called “spooky action at a distance.” He thought it meant quantum mechanics was incomplete. Experiments since the 1980s have confirmed it isn’t: entanglement is real, and the hidden-variable explanation doesn’t work.

title: 4  Entanglement
text:
4.6 Three-qubit entanglement — GHZ
The pattern extends. The GHZ state entangles three qubits:
\[|GHZ\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|000\rangle + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|111\rangle\]

ghz = new ket.Circuit(3).h(0).cx(0,1).cx(0,2)
svg(ghz.toSVG())
















pre(ghz.draw())







svg(ghz.simulate({ shots: 2000 }).toSVG())






Only \(|000\rangle\) and \(|111\rangle\). Measure any one qubit and the other two are determined. The bond entropies tell the full story:

ghz.bondEntropies()






Both bonds carry entanglement. The three qubits are collectively correlated across the whole register.
Now look at what the individual Bloch spheres show:

svg(ghz.blochSphere(0))







svg(ghz.blochSphere(1))







svg(ghz.blochSphere(2))






All three qubits are at the origin — maximally mixed individually, even though the joint state is pure. The information is entirely non-local: it exists only in the three-way correlation.

title: 4  Entanglement
text:
4.7 Entanglement as a resource
Entanglement isn’t just philosophically interesting — it’s a computational resource:

Quantum teleportation — transmit a qubit’s full state using only classical bits, via a shared Bell pair
Superdense coding — send two classical bits by physically transmitting one qubit
Quantum error correction — detect and fix errors without measuring the data directly
Every quantum speedup — Grover’s, Shor’s, and everything beyond — depends on building and exploiting entanglement across many qubits

The exponential state space from Chapter 3 is only useful because entanglement lets you act on all of it coherently. Without entanglement, a quantum computer is just a slow classical one.

title: 4  Entanglement
text:
4.8 What’s next
Chapter 5 combines interference and entanglement into the first real algorithm: Deutsch–Jozsa, a problem where a quantum computer beats any classical computer in a single query.

title: 5  Quantum Algorithms
text:
5.1 The problem
The ingredients are in place: superposition, single-qubit gates, multi-qubit states, entanglement. A quantum algorithm uses all of them together — amplifying the amplitudes of correct answers and cancelling the rest.
The first clean example is Deutsch–Jozsa.
You’re given a black-box function \(f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}\). You’re promised it’s either:
Classically, worst case requires \(2^{n-1}+1\) queries — you must check more than half the inputs. Quantum mechanics does it in one query.

title: 5  Quantum Algorithms
text:
Constant — same output for every input (all 0s or all 1s)
Balanced — exactly half the inputs map to 0, half to 1

title: 5  Quantum Algorithms
text:
5.2 The circuit
The phase oracle encodes \(f\) as a phase flip \((-1)^{f(x)}\) on each basis state \(|x\rangle\). The circuit is: H on all qubits → oracle → H on all qubits → measure.

dj = (n, oracle) => {
  let c = new ket.Circuit(n)
  for (let q = 0; q < n; q++) c = c.h(q)
  c = oracle(c)
  for (let q = 0; q < n; q++) c = c.h(q)
  return c
}

constantOracle = (c) => c
balancedOracle = (c) => c.cz(0, 1)

svg(dj(3, balancedOracle).toSVG())





























Constant oracle — all amplitude returns to \(|000\rangle\):

svg(dj(3, constantOracle).simulate({ shots: 500 }).toSVG())






Balanced oracle — \(|000\rangle\) amplitude cancels to zero:

svg(dj(3, balancedOracle).simulate({ shots: 500 }).toSVG())






One circuit, one measurement, certain answer.

title: 5  Quantum Algorithms
text:
5.3 Why it works
Apply H to all qubits: uniform superposition over all \(2^n\) inputs. The oracle applies phase \((-1)^{f(x)}\) to each \(|x\rangle\).
Constant: every state gets the same phase. The second H perfectly reverses the first — all amplitude flows back to \(|00\ldots0\rangle\).
Balanced: half the states get a phase flip. The symmetry is broken. \(|00\ldots0\rangle\) accumulates destructive interference — its amplitude cancels exactly to zero.
This is interference doing useful work: one global property determined by the coherent interaction of all \(2^n\) amplitudes simultaneously.

title: 5  Quantum Algorithms
text:
5.4 Bernstein–Vazirani
A closely related algorithm finds a hidden \(n\)-bit string \(s\) with a single query. The oracle computes \(f(x) = s \cdot x \pmod{2}\). The circuit is identical to Deutsch–Jozsa — the measurement directly reads out \(s\):

bvOracle = (c) => c.z(0).z(2)
svg(dj(3, bvOracle).simulate({ shots: 500 }).toSVG())















The measurement gives 101 with certainty. Classically: \(n\) queries. Quantum: one.

title: 5  Quantum Algorithms
text:
5.5 What’s next
Deutsch–Jozsa solves a contrived problem. Chapter 6 covers Grover’s algorithm — a quadratic speedup for unstructured search, applicable to any problem expressible as “find the input satisfying this condition.”

title: 6  Grover’s Search
text:
6.1 The idea
Search an unsorted list of \(N\) items for the one satisfying some condition. Classically: \(O(N)\) queries worst case. Grover’s algorithm: \(O(\sqrt{N})\) queries.
That’s a quadratic speedup, and it applies to any problem where you can write a function that recognises a correct answer.
Start in uniform superposition over all \(N = 2^n\) states. Each Grover iteration does two things:
After \(\approx \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N}\) iterations the marked amplitude is near 1. Measure and you get the answer.

title: 6  Grover’s Search
text:
Oracle: phase-flip the marked state — multiply its amplitude by \(-1\)
Diffusion: reflect all amplitudes around their average — amplifies the flipped state

title: 6  Grover’s Search
text:
6.2 Two qubits — searching 4 items
Searching for \(|11\rangle\). The oracle is a CZ (phase-flips \(|11\rangle\)). One iteration suffices:

oracle_11 = (c) => c.cz(0, 1)
g2 = ket.grover(2, oracle_11, 1)
svg(g2.toSVG())























svg(g2.simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())






\(|11\rangle\) with certainty. One oracle call, one item in four.

title: 6  Grover’s Search
text:
6.3 Three qubits — searching 8 items
Searching for \(|101\rangle\). The oracle flips the middle qubit to convert \(|101\rangle \to |111\rangle\), applies a multi-controlled phase flip, then undoes:

oracle_101 = (c) => c.x(1).h(2).ccx(0, 1, 2).h(2).x(1)
g3 = ket.grover(3, oracle_101)   // optimal iterations chosen automatically
svg(g3.toSVG())























svg(g3.simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())






\(|101\rangle\) dominates. Optimal iterations for \(n=3\): \(\approx\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{8} \approx 2\).

title: 6  Grover’s Search
text:
6.4 Over-iterating
Grover is a rotation, not a one-way boost. Iterate past the optimum and the probability cycles back down:

g3_over = ket.grover(3, oracle_101, 5)
svg(g3_over.simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())















At 5 iterations — past the optimum of 2 for \(n=3\) — the probability of \(|101\rangle\) has decayed from ~93% back toward the noise floor. Stopping at the right point is part of the algorithm.

title: 6  Grover’s Search
section: 6.5 What Grover can and can’t do
text:
6.5 What Grover can and can’t do
Grover provides a provable \(\sqrt{N}\) speedup for unstructured search. It speeds up brute-force components of many classical problems: constraint satisfaction, collision finding, key search.
What it can’t do: provide an exponential speedup. Breaking a 128-bit symmetric key classically costs \(2^{128}\) operations. With Grover: \(2^{64}\) — still astronomical. Symmetric cryptography needs longer keys in a quantum world, not redesign.
Shor’s algorithm, next, does achieve an exponential speedup — but only for structured problems like factoring.

title: 6  Grover’s Search
text:
6.6 What’s next
Grover’s speedup comes from amplitude amplification. Shor’s exponential speedup requires a more powerful subroutine: the Quantum Fourier Transform. Chapter 7 builds it.

title: 7  The Quantum Fourier Transform
text:
7.1 What it does
The classical Fourier Transform decomposes a signal into its constituent frequencies. The Quantum Fourier Transform does the same to quantum amplitudes — and it’s the engine behind Shor’s algorithm.
The key difference from the classical FFT: the QFT on \(n\) qubits uses \(O(n^2)\) gates, while the best classical FFT on \(2^n\) data points needs \(O(n \cdot 2^n)\) operations. Exponentially fewer gates.
The catch: you can’t read out the transformed amplitudes directly — measurement collapses them. The QFT is useful as a subroutine that restructures phases so subsequent gates can extract what you need.
The QFT maps each basis state to a uniform superposition with phases encoding the input:
\[\text{QFT}|j\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}} \sum_{k=0}^{2^n-1} e^{2\pi i jk/2^n} |k\rangle\]
Every output state has equal amplitude — measurement after a bare QFT is uniform. The information is in the phases, which interfere with subsequent gates.

title: 7  The Quantum Fourier Transform
7  The Quantum Fourier Transform
7  The Quantum Fourier Transform
text:
7.4 Connection to Shor’s
Shor’s algorithm reduces factoring to period finding: given \(f(x) = a^x \bmod N\), find its period \(r\). Period finding is phase estimation on the unitary \(U_a|x\rangle = |ax \bmod N\rangle\) — its eigenvalues encode \(1/r\).
Building the circuit for \(U_a\) is the hard part (the Beauregard circuit). Once you have it, QPE extracts the period, and from the period, classical arithmetic gives the factors. Chapter 8 runs the whole thing.

title: 8  Shor’s Algorithm
text:
8.1 Why factoring matters
In 1994, Peter Shor showed that a quantum computer can factor large integers in polynomial time. This broke the assumption underpinning RSA encryption and started the modern era of quantum computing research.
RSA security rests on a simple asymmetry: multiplying two large primes is easy, factoring their product is hard. The best known classical algorithm runs in roughly \(e^{O(n^{1/3})}\) time for an \(n\)-bit number. Shor’s algorithm runs in \(O(n^3)\) — polynomial. A large enough quantum computer breaks RSA.

title: 8  Shor’s Algorithm
text:
8.2 The reduction
Shor doesn’t factor directly. It reduces factoring to period finding:

Pick random \(a < N\) with \(\gcd(a, N) = 1\)
Find period \(r\) of \(f(x) = a^x \bmod N\)
Then \(\gcd(a^{r/2} \pm 1,\, N)\) gives the factors (if \(r\) is even and \(a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1\))

Steps 1 and 3 are classical. Step 2 is quantum — period finding via phase estimation on the unitary \(U_a|x\rangle = |ax \bmod N\rangle\).

title: 8  Shor’s Algorithm
text:
8.3 Running it
shorBeauregard implements the full gate-decomposed Beauregard circuit:

r15 = ket.shorBeauregard(15n, 7n)
pre(`factors = ${r15.factors.map(String).join(' \xd7 ')}  (base ${r15.a}, ${r15.qubits} qubits)`)















The algorithm selects the most efficient base internally. Here it factors 15 into 3 and 5 using 19 qubits.

r21 = ket.shorBeauregard(21n, 2n)
pre(`21 = ${r21.factors.map(String).join(' \xd7 ')}  (${r21.qubits} qubits)`)
















r35 = ket.shorBeauregard(35n, 3n)
pre(`35 = ${r35.factors.map(String).join(' \xd7 ')}  (${r35.qubits} qubits)`)

title: 8  Shor’s Algorithm
text:
8.4 The qubit cost
The Beauregard circuit for factoring \(N\) requires \(O(\log N)\) qubits. For \(N=15\): 19 qubits. For a 2048-bit RSA key: roughly 4000 logical qubits, plus thousands more for error correction. Current hardware has hundreds of noisy physical qubits.
The algorithm works. The hardware isn’t there yet.

title: 8  Shor’s Algorithm
text:
8.5 Simulation limits
The full gate-decomposed Beauregard circuit is expensive to simulate classically — intermediate entanglement grows with \(n\), requiring \(O(\chi^2)\) work per gate where \(\chi\) is the MPS bond dimension:

Beyond N ≈ 77 the full Beauregard circuit becomes impractical to simulate exactly. The demo below takes a different path.

title: 8  Shor’s Algorithm
8  Shor’s Algorithm
text:
8.7 What’s next
All the circuits so far assumed perfect gates. Chapter 9 covers noise: what goes wrong on real hardware and how ket models it.

title: 9  Noise and Real Hardware
text:
9.1 Decoherence
Every circuit in the previous chapters ran perfectly. Real quantum hardware doesn’t.
Qubits are physical objects — superconducting circuits, trapped ions, photons. They interact with their environment, and that interaction corrupts the quantum state. Understanding noise is the difference between a textbook circuit and one that works in practice.
A qubit’s coherence is its ability to maintain superposition. Two timescales govern how quickly it’s lost:
\(T_1\) — relaxation time: the qubit spontaneously decays from \(|1\rangle\) to \(|0\rangle\), like an excited atom emitting a photon. Energy leaks to the environment.
\(T_2\) — dephasing time: the phase relationship between \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) randomises, collapsing superposition without flipping the bit. Always \(T_2 \leq 2T_1\).
A circuit’s total runtime must be well below both timescales or errors accumulate faster than computation.

title: 9  Noise and Real Hardware
text:
9.2 Simulating noise
Pass a noise profile to run() to apply \(T_1\)/\(T_2\) decay. The same Bell state, clean vs noisy:

bell = new ket.Circuit(2).h(0).cx(0, 1)
svg(bell.simulate({ shots: 2000 }).toSVG())
















svg(bell.run({ shots: 2000, noise: { t1: 50, t2: 30 } }).toSVG())






The clean Bell state shows only \(|00\rangle\) and \(|11\rangle\). The noisy run leaks into \(|01\rangle\) and \(|10\rangle\) — decoherence partially collapses the entanglement during the circuit.
Stronger decoherence (\(T_1\) and \(T_2\) measured in microseconds; shorter means noisier):

svg(bell.run({ shots: 2000, noise: { t1: 10, t2: 5 } }).toSVG())






At \(T_1 = 10\,\mu\text{s}\), the correlation is almost entirely destroyed. The histogram looks nearly uniform — noise has randomised the result.

title: 9  Noise and Real Hardware
text:
9.3 Circuit depth matters
A shallower circuit has less time to decohere. The same identity operation at different depths:

shallow = new ket.Circuit(1).h(0).h(0)   // H·H = I, depth 2
svg(shallow.run({ shots: 2000, noise: { t1: 100, t2: 50 } }).toSVG())
















deep = (() => { let c = new ket.Circuit(1); for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) c = c.h(0); return c })()
svg(deep.run({ shots: 2000, noise: { t1: 100, t2: 50 } }).toSVG())















Both are mathematically identity — they should always return \(|0\rangle\). The deep circuit leaks into \(|1\rangle\) substantially more. More time in the circuit means more exposure to noise.

title: 9  Noise and Real Hardware
text:
9.4 Real device profiles
ket ships with noise models calibrated from real hardware:

pre(Object.keys(ket.DEVICES).join('\n'))







svg(bell.run({ shots: 2000, noise: "harmony" }).toSVG())







svg(bell.run({ shots: 2000, noise: "ibm_sherbrooke" }).toSVG())






Different hardware, different error profiles. IonQ’s trapped-ion systems tend to have higher gate fidelity but slower gate times. IBM’s superconducting systems are faster but noisier per gate. The device string selects the full calibrated noise model including \(T_1\), \(T_2\), gate error rates, and readout error.

title: 9  Noise and Real Hardware
text:
9.5 Readout error mitigation
Not all noise happens during the circuit. Measurement itself is imperfect: a qubit in \(|0\rangle\) occasionally registers as 1, and vice versa. This is readout error — it’s separate from decoherence and can be corrected after the fact.
run() accepts readoutMitigation: true to apply a simple matrix inversion correction:

svg(bell.run({ shots: 2000, noise: "harmony" }).toSVG())







svg(bell.run({ shots: 2000, noise: "harmony", readoutMitigation: true }).toSVG())






The mitigated histogram is closer to the ideal \(|00\rangle\)/\(|11\rangle\) split. The correction is linear: the simulator estimates the readout error matrix from the device profile and inverts it. It doesn’t fix decoherence — only the measurement step — but on current hardware, readout error is often the dominant source of error for short circuits.

title: 9  Noise and Real Hardware
text:
9.6 Error correction (the idea)
The solution to decoherence is quantum error correction (QEC): encode one logical qubit across several physical qubits so that any single error can be detected and corrected without measuring — and thus collapsing — the data.
The simplest example: the three-qubit bit-flip code encodes \(|0\rangle \to |000\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle \to |111\rangle\). A single bit-flip is detectable by comparing pairs — majority vote restores the original.
Full QEC requires 50–1000 physical qubits per logical qubit depending on the code and target error rate. The algorithms in Chapters 6–8 assume perfect logical qubits. Getting there is the work of the next decade.

title: 9  Noise and Real Hardware
9  Noise and Real Hardware
text:
9.8 What’s next
The final chapter applies quantum circuits to their original motivation: simulating physics. Hamiltonians, Trotterisation, and the Variational Quantum Eigensolver.

title: 10  Hamiltonians and Quantum Simulation
text:
10.1 Hamiltonians as Pauli strings
Feynman’s original motivation for quantum computers was simulation: classical computers are exponentially slow at simulating quantum systems. A quantum computer, being quantum itself, should be able to do it efficiently.
A Hamiltonian is the operator that governs a quantum system’s energy and time evolution. Finding its lowest-energy state — the ground state — answers questions in chemistry, materials science, and drug discovery that classical computers can’t reach.
Any Hamiltonian on \(n\) qubits can be written as a sum of Pauli operator products:
\[H = \sum_i c_i \; P_i\]
where each \(P_i\) is a tensor product of \(I, X, Y, Z\) across qubits — a Pauli string. In ket, each term is { ops: 'ZZ', coeff: -1.0 } where the string encodes the Pauli on each qubit.

title: 10  Hamiltonians and Quantum Simulation
text:
10.2 Trotter simulation
To simulate time evolution \(|\psi(t)\rangle = e^{-iHt}|\psi(0)\rangle\), we use Trotterisation: split time into small steps \(\Delta t\) and apply each Pauli term separately per step:
\[e^{-iHt} \approx \left(\prod_i e^{-ic_i P_i \Delta t}\right)^{N_\text{steps}}\]
Evolving a single qubit under \(H = X\) — starting in \(|0\rangle\), at \(t = \pi/2\) the state reaches \(|1\rangle\) with certainty (a full population inversion):

H_x = [{ ops: 'X', coeff: 1.0 }]
trot = ket.trotter(1, H_x, Math.PI / 2, 8)
svg(trot.toSVG())























evolution = new ket.Circuit(1).compose(trot)
svg(evolution.simulate({ shots: 500 }).toSVG())















\(|0\rangle\) has been driven to \(|1\rangle\) by the Hamiltonian — the quantum analogue of Rabi oscillations in a two-level atom.

title: 10  Hamiltonians and Quantum Simulation
text:
10.3 The Variational Quantum Eigensolver
VQE is a hybrid classical-quantum algorithm for ground state energies, designed for near-term hardware with shallow, noise-tolerant circuits.
Parameterise a circuit (the ansatz), measure the expectation value \(\langle\psi(\theta)|H|\psi(\theta)\rangle\), and use a classical optimiser to minimise it. By the variational principle the minimum is an upper bound on the true ground state energy.
For \(H = Z\) the ground state is \(|1\rangle\) with energy \(-1\):

H_single = [{ ops: 'Z', coeff: 1.0 }]
ansatz_1q = (params) => new ket.Circuit(1).ry(params[0], 0)
result_1q = ket.minimize(ansatz_1q, H_single, [0.1])
pre(`Ground state energy: ${result_1q.energy.toFixed(6)}   (exact: -1.0)\nOptimal \u03b8:           ${result_1q.params[0].toFixed(6)} rad  (= \u03c0)`)





























The optimiser finds \(\theta = \pi\) — ry(π) maps \(|0\rangle \to |1\rangle\). Energy \(-1\), exact.

title: 10  Hamiltonians and Quantum Simulation
text:
10.4 A two-qubit molecule
A simplified model of the hydrogen molecule H₂ near its equilibrium bond length fits in a two-qubit Hamiltonian. The coefficients come from quantum chemistry:

H_h2 = [
  { ops: 'II', coeff: -0.8105 },
  { ops: 'ZI', coeff:  0.1722 },
  { ops: 'IZ', coeff: -0.2228 },
  { ops: 'ZZ', coeff:  0.1201 },
  { ops: 'XX', coeff:  0.1686 },
]

ansatz_2q = (params) =>
  new ket.Circuit(2).ry(params[0], 0).ry(params[1], 1).cx(0, 1)

result_2q = ket.minimize(ansatz_2q, H_h2, [0.1, 0.1])
pre(`H\u2082 ground state energy: ${result_2q.energy.toFixed(6)} Hartree\nOptimal params:         [${result_2q.params.map(p => p.toFixed(3)).join(', ')}]`)





























Ground state energy of H₂ from a quantum circuit, found by optimising two rotation angles. For larger molecules — where the classical simulation becomes intractable — this is the kind of calculation quantum computers are expected to accelerate dramatically.

title: 10  Hamiltonians and Quantum Simulation
text:
10.5 QAOA — optimization on graphs
The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm applies the same hybrid idea to combinatorial problems. Where VQE finds ground state energies, QAOA finds approximate solutions to optimization problems like Max-Cut: partition a graph’s nodes into two sets to maximise the number of edges between them.
The ansatz alternates between a problem Hamiltonian \(e^{-i\gamma H_C}\) (which encodes the objective) and a mixing Hamiltonian \(e^{-i\beta H_B}\) (which explores solutions). Depth \(p\) means \(p\) rounds of each.
A 4-node square graph has two optimal cuts — alternating nodes \(0101\) and \(1010\), each severing all 4 edges:

qaoa_edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[3,0]]
H_maxcut = ket.maxCutHamiltonian(4, qaoa_edges)
















ansatz_qaoa1 = (params) => ket.qaoa(4, qaoa_edges, [params[0]], [params[1]])
result_qaoa1 = ket.minimize(ansatz_qaoa1, H_maxcut, [0.3, 0.7])
svg(ansatz_qaoa1(result_qaoa1.params).simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())























ansatz_qaoa2 = (params) => ket.qaoa(4, qaoa_edges, [params[0], params[1]], [params[2], params[3]])
result_qaoa2 = ket.minimize(ansatz_qaoa2, H_maxcut, [0.3, 0.6, 0.7, 0.4])
svg(ansatz_qaoa2(result_qaoa2.params).simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())






















At \(p=1\) the optimal states get a modest boost. At \(p=2\), 0101 and 1010 dominate — the circuit has learned to concentrate probability on the two maximum cuts. More layers means a better approximation; in the limit \(p \to \infty\), QAOA finds the exact optimum.

pre(`p=1 energy: ${result_qaoa1.energy.toFixed(4)}   p=2 energy: ${result_qaoa2.energy.toFixed(4)}   (max cut = 4)`)






The energy rises toward 4 with depth. This is the variational principle at work on a combinatorial problem — the same machinery as VQE, applied to graphs instead of molecules.

title: 10  Hamiltonians and Quantum Simulation
text:
10.6 Where this is going
The circuits in this book run on a simulator. The algorithms are correct; the hardware to run them at useful scale is still being built.
The near-term roadmap:

NISQ era (now): 100–1000 noisy qubits. VQE, QAOA, quantum ML — shallow circuits that tolerate noise.
Early fault-tolerant (~5–10 years): logical qubits via error correction. First practical advantage for quantum chemistry and optimisation.
Full fault-tolerant (~15+ years): millions of physical qubits. Shor’s at cryptographic scale, full Hamiltonian simulation of useful molecules.

The mathematics in this book is complete. The engineering is the work of the next decade.

title: 11  Backends and Classical Control
11  Backends and Classical Control
text:
11.2 Mid-circuit measurement and classical control
Every circuit so far measured at the end. ket supports measuring qubits mid-circuit and using the classical result to conditionally apply gates — the same feedback loop used in quantum error correction and teleportation.

c_midmeas = new ket.Circuit(2)
  .h(0)
  .measure(0, 'm', 0)
  .if('m', 1, c => c.x(1))
svg(c_midmeas.toSVG())
















svg(c_midmeas.simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())






Qubit 0 is measured. If it came out 1, qubit 1 is flipped. The result is always \(|00\rangle\) or \(|11\rangle\) — the two qubits are forced to agree by classical feedback, even though they were never entangled.

11.2.1 Quantum teleportation
The canonical application of mid-circuit measurement is quantum teleportation: transmitting a qubit’s full quantum state using only classical bits and a pre-shared entangled pair.
The protocol:

Alice and Bob share a Bell pair (qubits 1 and 2)
Alice holds the qubit to teleport (qubit 0)
Alice entangles her qubit with her half of the Bell pair and measures both
Alice sends her two classical measurement bits to Bob
Bob applies conditional X and Z corrections to his qubit

The state of qubit 0 arrives at qubit 2 — no quantum channel, just two classical bits.

tele = new ket.Circuit(3)
  .x(0)                         // state to teleport: |1⟩
  .h(1).cx(1, 2)                // Bell pair on qubits 1 and 2
  .cx(0, 1).h(0)                // Alice's Bell-basis measurement
  .measure(0, 'm0', 0)
  .measure(1, 'm1', 0)
  .if('m1', 1, c => c.x(2))    // Bob's correction: X if m1 = 1
  .if('m0', 1, c => c.z(2))    // Bob's correction: Z if m0 = 1
svg(tele.toSVG())
















svg(tele.simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())






Alice’s measurement outcomes (\(m_0\), \(m_1\)) are random and uniformly distributed across all four combinations. But qubit 2 — Bob’s qubit — is always \(|1\rangle\) regardless of which outcome Alice got. The corrections steer it to the right state every time.
This is what makes teleportation remarkable: the quantum information travels without a quantum channel. The two classical bits tell Bob which of four correction operations to apply, and after applying it, he holds the original state exactly.

title: 11  Backends and Classical Control
text:
11.3 Quantum error correction
Mid-circuit measurement makes quantum error correction (QEC) possible. The idea: encode one logical qubit across several physical qubits, measure parities (not values) to detect errors, then correct without ever touching the logical state.
The simplest code is the 3-qubit bit-flip code:

Encode: \(|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\) → \(\alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle\)
Two syndrome ancillas measure \(Z_0Z_1\) and \(Z_1Z_2\) — the parity of adjacent qubit pairs
Any single bit-flip changes exactly two parities, uniquely identifying which qubit flipped
Classical control corrects the right qubit; the logical state is unchanged


qec_error = new ket.Circuit(5)
  .h(0)                                      // logical |+⟩ to protect
  .cx(0, 1).cx(0, 2)                         // encode
  .x(1)                                      // inject error: flip qubit 1
  .cx(0, 3).cx(1, 3).measure(3, 's', 0)     // syndrome: parity(q0,q1) → s[0]
  .cx(1, 4).cx(2, 4).measure(4, 's', 1)     // syndrome: parity(q1,q2) → s[1]
  .if('s', 1, c => c.x(0))                  // s=01 → correct q0
  .if('s', 3, c => c.x(1))                  // s=11 → correct q1
  .if('s', 2, c => c.x(2))                  // s=10 → correct q2
  .cx(0, 1).cx(0, 2)                        // decode
svg(qec_error.toSVG())
















svg(qec_error.simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())






The histogram shows only two outcomes — qubit 0 is 50/50 (the original \(|+\rangle\) recovered), qubits 1 and 2 are always \(|0\rangle\) after decoding, and the syndrome ancillas (qubits 3 and 4) are always \(|11\rangle\), confirming that a qubit-1 error was detected and corrected every shot.
Compare the clean case — no error injected:

qec_clean = new ket.Circuit(5)
  .h(0)
  .cx(0, 1).cx(0, 2)
  .cx(0, 3).cx(1, 3).measure(3, 's', 0)
  .cx(1, 4).cx(2, 4).measure(4, 's', 1)
  .if('s', 1, c => c.x(0))
  .if('s', 3, c => c.x(1))
  .if('s', 2, c => c.x(2))
  .cx(0, 1).cx(0, 2)
svg(qec_clean.simulate({ shots: 1000 }).toSVG())















Syndrome ancillas are \(|00\rangle\) — no error detected. Logical qubit 0 is still \(|+\rangle\). The parity measurements extracted error information without disturbing the encoded data.
This is the principle behind every fault-tolerant quantum computer: errors are detectable and correctable because the logical state is spread across multiple qubits, and syndromes can be measured without collapsing the logical superposition.

title: 11  Backends and Classical Control
text:
11.4 Custom noise channels
The T1/T2 model from Chapter 9 describes thermal relaxation and dephasing. But real hardware has many other error types. run() accepts custom Kraus operators — the most general way to describe any quantum channel.
A Kraus channel \(\mathcal{E}(\rho) = \sum_k K_k \rho K_k^\dagger\) is valid whenever \(\sum_k K_k^\dagger K_k = I\). The simulator applies the channel after each single-qubit gate (pass kraus1) or two-qubit gate (pass kraus2).
Amplitude damping models energy loss to the environment — a qubit in \(|1\rangle\) spontaneously decays to \(|0\rangle\) with probability \(\gamma\):
\[K_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{1-\gamma} \end{pmatrix} \qquad K_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sqrt{\gamma} \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\]

c_kraus = (re, im = 0) => ({ re, im })

// Amplitude damping: qubit decays from |1⟩ to |0⟩ with probability gamma per gate
gamma_low  = 0.05
gamma_high = 0.40

K0_low  = [[c_kraus(1), c_kraus(0)], [c_kraus(0), c_kraus(Math.sqrt(1 - gamma_low))]]
K1_low  = [[c_kraus(0), c_kraus(Math.sqrt(gamma_low))],  [c_kraus(0), c_kraus(0)]]
K0_high = [[c_kraus(1), c_kraus(0)], [c_kraus(0), c_kraus(Math.sqrt(1 - gamma_high))]]
K1_high = [[c_kraus(0), c_kraus(Math.sqrt(gamma_high))], [c_kraus(0), c_kraus(0)]]



















































circ_damp = new ket.Circuit(1).x(0)
svg(circ_damp.run({ shots: 2000, noise: { kraus1: [K0_low,  K1_low]  } }).toSVG())
















svg(circ_damp.run({ shots: 2000, noise: { kraus1: [K0_high, K1_high] } }).toSVG())






At \(\gamma = 0.05\) most population stays in \(|1\rangle\). At \(\gamma = 0.40\) the decay is severe — the energy loss dominates. Amplitude damping is not captured by dephasing alone: T2 noise randomises the phase but doesn’t move population between \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\). Kraus operators let you model both independently.
Phase damping — pure dephasing with no energy loss — has its own Kraus form. You can also describe coherent errors, leakage to non-computational states, or any other physically motivated noise. The constraint is just \(\sum_k K_k^\dagger K_k = I\).

title: 11  Backends and Classical Control
text:
11.5 What this means
The backend architecture reflects a real partition in quantum computing:

Clifford circuits are classically simulable. They don’t give quantum advantage. They’re useful for error correction codes and benchmarking — but not for computation.
Non-Clifford circuits (T gates, Toffoli, controlled rotations) escape classical simulation and are where quantum advantage lives.
Low-entanglement circuits (small \(\chi\)) can be handled by MPS regardless of qubit count.
Noisy circuits require density matrix simulation — the state is now a \(2^n \times 2^n\) matrix, not a vector.

Mid-circuit measurement and classical control bridge classical and quantum computation — they’re how error-corrected logical qubits are implemented in practice, where syndrome measurements drive real-time correction without disturbing the data.

text:
Math notation glossary







Symbol
Meaning




\(\vert\psi\rangle\)
Quantum state (ket)


\(\langle\psi\vert\)
Conjugate transpose (bra)


\(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}\)
Complex amplitudes


\(\vert\alpha\vert^2\)
Measurement probability


\(\otimes\)
Tensor product


\(U^\dagger\)
Conjugate transpose (inverse unitary)


\(\langle H\rangle = \langle\psi\vert H\vert\psi\rangle\)
Expectation value


\(\chi\)
MPS bond dimension


\(S_\text{vN}\)
Von Neumann entanglement entropy
